target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is justified because it is a core, hands-on biology activity and often uses already-dead animals.
objection: AG2 argues that those points do not justify killing animals for school use, because most dissection animals are reportedly wild-caught, and that catching them harms ecosystems by reducing local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG1’s assumption that students need animal dissection to meet biology or medical-training requirements.
objection: AG2 says dissection is not required by major standards such as AP Biology or the Next Generation Science Standards, and that U.S. and Canadian medical training does not rely on animal dissection, so the educational necessity claim is unsupported.

target: AG1’s claim that real animal dissection provides uniquely valuable learning that alternatives cannot match.
objection: AG2 objects that synthetic models and computer simulations can teach anatomy and physiology just as well or better, while allowing repetition and zooming without the moral cost of using dead animals.

target: AG1’s idea that “hands-on” biology requires animal dissection specifically.
objection: AG2 argues that hands-on scientific learning can still happen with alternatives, since students can practice observation, labeling, and reasoning without using dead or killed animals.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection animals are mostly wild-caught and that schools should therefore ban dissection outright.
objection: AG1 disputes the 99% wild-caught claim as not fitting the common classroom case, arguing that many specimens are already-dead byproducts such as fetal pigs from the meat industry, and that schools can solve sourcing concerns through approved-vendor procurement rather than a blanket ban.

target: AG2’s argument that dissection is unnecessary because it is not mandated by standards.
objection: AG1 responds that schools teach valuable skills beyond minimum standards, and that dissection uniquely develops real-lab competencies such as careful observation, spatial understanding of organs, and adapting to biological tissue in ways screens cannot fully replicate.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives work just as well and are equally accessible.
objection: AG1 argues that this assumes equal access to high-quality models and software, which many districts lack; therefore dissection can be a more equitable and practical hands-on option than premium digital alternatives.

target: AG1’s proposed fix of “responsible procurement” for specimens.
objection: AG2 says procurement is not a convincing solution because schools cannot reliably guarantee that all specimens avoid wild capture or other harmful sourcing, and buying more specimens can still support supply chains that expand harmful production or capture.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection’s tactile experience justifies keeping it.
objection: AG2 argues that the educational gains are not worth the ethical and environmental costs when alternatives can achieve the same learning goals, often with better repeatability and review.

target: AG1’s claim that opt-out roles make dissection inclusive.
objection: AG2 says that letting some students opt out does not make the practice truly inclusive, because the class still centers on an activity built around animal death and forces unwilling students to accommodate it.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection still fuels harmful supply chains even when specimens are byproducts.
objection: AG1 counters that, in the common case of meat-industry byproducts destined for landfill, school purchases do not create additional killing and instead redirect material that would otherwise be discarded.

target: AG2’s objection that opt-out participation is not truly inclusive.
objection: AG1 says inclusion can be handled by assigning alternative but equivalent roles—such as labeling, diagramming, guided observation, or measurement—so students who do not want to dissect can still meet the same learning goals.

target: AG1’s claim that opt-out roles create equivalent learning and that byproduct sourcing avoids harm.
objection: AG2 argues that opt-out accommodation still leaves dissection as the classroom norm and does not provide truly equivalent access to the central spatial and procedural experience; AG2 also says byproduct sourcing may still create market demand that incentivizes supply, so it is not a moral guarantee.

target: AG2’s claim that opt-out inclusion still makes dissection ethically unacceptable.
objection: AG1 responds that equivalent roles can preserve learning outcomes while respecting students who decline dissection, so inclusion does not require eliminating the activity for everyone.

target: AG2’s claim that byproduct procurement still incentivizes harmful supply.
objection: AG1 argues that if specimens are true byproducts of an existing meat-processing stream, schools are not driving the animals’ killing; they are only using material that already exists and would otherwise be discarded.

target: AG2’s claim that motivation is not a sufficient reason to keep dissection.
objection: AG1 adds that dissection can create strong “aha” moments and motivate students toward science careers, especially those who may not engage as deeply with digital content.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is authentic science because it involves real tissue variability and procedural judgment.
objection: AG2 says those competencies are not unique to animal dissection and can be taught with non-animal alternatives such as synthetic models, 3D-printed materials, virtual labs, and non-animal wet-lab substitutes.

target: AG1’s claim that teaching students where specimens come from makes the practice ethically acceptable.
objection: AG2 argues that ethics instruction cannot neutralize the moral problem that the activity itself is built around harming animals, and that ethics can be taught without dissection.

target: AG2’s argument that precaution requires a full ban because sourcing is uncertain and animal harm is irreversible.
objection: AG1 says precaution supports risk management rather than prohibition: schools can use verified, documented byproduct sources, so the ethical risk becomes narrowly controlled instead of requiring a blanket ban.

target: AG2’s argument that non-animal alternatives are enough because they meet learning goals.
objection: AG1 says that, even if alternatives teach anatomy concepts, they do not fully replicate the unique experience of real tissue, spatial relations, procedural judgment, and other skills learned in actual dissection.

target: AG2’s claim that waste-management concerns do not justify dissection.
objection: AG1 argues that if animals are already dead and headed for disposal, banning dissection merely increases landfill or incineration while sacrificing a high-impact educational activity, so the waste tradeoff matters.

target: AG1’s “harm-reduction proportionality” defense of dissection using byproducts and verified suppliers.
objection: AG2 responds that precaution should still apply because schools cannot reliably verify every supply chain, the harms are irreversible, and if non-animal alternatives can achieve the same educational outcomes, schools should not create additional demand for animal use.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection should be preserved because it is a distinctive hands-on option and can be ethically managed.
objection: AG2 says the issue is not merely whether dissection can be made less bad; it is that students should not dissect animals at all because it is not required by standards, medical training does not depend on it, and effective alternatives already exist without animal or ecological harm.

target: AG1’s appeal to “verified byproduct sourcing” and opt-out pathways.
objection: AG2 argues that even verified sourcing does not solve the core problem, because the practice still uses animals unnecessarily when effective alternatives exist, and if the same learning outcomes can be achieved without dissection, the practice is ethically avoidable.

target: AG2’s claim that equivalent outputs from non-dissection pathways show dissection is unnecessary.
objection: AG1 says “unnecessary” depends on broader educational goals, because dissection teaches authentic science skills—such as handling tissue variability, making procedural decisions, and developing lab judgment—that alternatives may not fully reproduce, while also creating motivational “aha” moments.

target: AG2’s assumption that equal assessment outputs mean dissection should be eliminated.
objection: AG1 argues that schools can preserve the option for students who want the full hands-on experience while allowing others to use alternative pathways, so the presence of comparable outputs does not eliminate dissection’s distinct educational value.
